rows.sourceExcerpt:
E Adoption was not immediate. Institutions had invested in competing raised systems, teachers differed over methods, and authorities did not automatically accept a code created by a young blind student. Braille continued refining the system and extended it for music and mathematics. He died in 1852 without seeing the full international reach of his work. Over time, practical use by readers and writers supplied an argument that official preference could not easily dismiss. The system spread through schools and libraries, although languages developed their own conventions. Its success was therefore not a single moment of invention followed by instant agreement; it was a process of testing, teaching, adaptation and institutional change.

F The same design principle survived changes in production. A mechanical braillewriter uses six main keys corresponding to the cell's dots. Embossers can produce pages from digital files, while refreshable displays raise and lower pins so that electronic text can be read line by line. These devices alter speed, storage and distribution, but they do not make the tactile code obsolete. A digital document still needs rules that tell a display which dot pattern represents a character or symbol. Nor has technology removed every constraint: embossed volumes occupy substantial space, refreshable equipment can be costly, and transcription must represent layouts, mathematics and music accurately rather than convert ordinary print mechanically.

G The history also warns against measuring an accessible system only by resemblance to the dominant one. Raised print preserved the appearance of letters but imposed a heavy perceptual burden on touch. The dot cell changed the design question from 'How can print be felt?' to 'What can a fingertip distinguish quickly and what can a writer produce directly?' That shift joined finger span, page economy and independent composition in one solution. Modern audio and speech tools offer valuable additional access, yet they serve different purposes from spelling, punctuation and close textual study. The continuing use of braille reflects not resistance to new technology but the value of a code designed around active literacy rather than passive receipt. It endures.

responseBinding.questionText: Question 30

rows.sourceExcerpt: F Researchers quantify the balance with a net cooling power. Outgoing thermal radiation is counted as a gain for cooling; absorbed sunlight, downward atmospheric radiation and non-radiative heat transfer count against it. Each term changes with surface temperature and conditions, so a single efficiency percentage can conceal important assumptions. A test conducted at night removes the largest solar term and is useful for studying emission, but it cannot establish daytime performance by itself. Likewise, reporting only a surface temperature without a reference surface makes weather effects difficult to separate. Strong evidence clearly combines spectral measurements, an energy-balance model and outdoor comparisons.

Thus a claim that a film reflects a certain fraction of sunlight is a statement about the material, not yet a statement about energy bills, comfort or public-health benefit.

responseBinding.questionText: Question 33

rows.sourceExcerpt: H This layered reasoning explains both the promise and the caution surrounding radiative cooling. The physical mechanism is real: a surface can send heat through a spectral opening while resisting solar gain. Yet the magnitude of that effect moves through a chain—from optical spectrum, to surface energy balance, to roof construction, to indoor conditions, and finally to human or energy outcomes. A useful diagram should keep these levels distinct. It should show incoming sunlight meeting a reflective layer, thermal emission leaving the surface through the atmospheric window, and conductive exchange moderated by insulation above the roof deck. It should not imply that every emitted ray reaches space or that a cooler coating guarantees an equally large reduction inside.

responseBinding.questionText: Question 34

rows.sourceExcerpt: A A roof under a clear sky participates in two energy exchanges that are easy to confuse. Sunlight arrives mainly at short wavelengths and can heat the surface if absorbed. The warm surface also emits energy at longer, thermal-infrared wavelengths. Ordinary materials may lose some heat by this second route at night, when solar input has disappeared. Achieving cooling in daytime is harder because even modest absorption of intense sunlight can exceed the infrared loss. A successful passive cooling surface must therefore perform two apparently separate optical tasks: reject most incoming solar energy and emit thermal radiation strongly in the wavelengths through which that radiation can escape.

responseBinding.questionText: Dog’s name: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: His name is Bramble — B R A M B L E. The receptionist at our old clinic once wrote Brandon, so I always spell it now.

responseBinding.questionText: Breed: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: They wondered whether he had some collie in him, but every official page says lurcher. So please put lurcher.

responseBinding.questionText: Age: ______ years

bindings.audiblePhrase: We do know it. He turned three in January. His adoption form still says two, but that was completed before his birthday.

responseBinding.questionText: Final four microchip digits: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: I've found it. The photocopy ends four, two, eight, seven, but someone switched the middle digits. The original certificate ends four, eight, two, seven — that's 4827 on the form.

responseBinding.questionText: Previous vaccination month: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: Yes, it was in March. We adopted him in February, then the rescue centre arranged the vaccination the following month.

responseBinding.questionText: Preferred confirmation method: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: A text message would be best. I rarely hear my phone while I'm working, and clinic emails sometimes disappear into the junk folder, but I check texts at lunch.

responseBinding.questionText: Which clinic location does Niamh choose?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: the mobile clinic beside the library

bindings.audiblePhrase: I'll choose the mobile clinic beside the library. Parking near the main surgery is difficult, and the school is across the city. The library is a short walk from my office, so I can bring Bramble over after work.

responseBinding.questionText: Why does Niamh reject the earlier appointments?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Bramble is fine in the morning, and transport isn't the issue. I have a work meeting that runs until three, so the two earlier times are impossible. Four-forty-five is the one I can manage.

responseBinding.questionText: What must Niamh bring to the appointment?

bindings.audiblePhrase: I've booked that. Please arrive ten minutes early and bring his vaccination record, even though some entries came from the rescue centre. We can scan the chip at the van, so the chip certificate is optional, and we don't need proof of address.

responseBinding.questionText: How will Niamh pay the clinic fee?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Good. Payment is taken at the van, and you can pay by card when you arrive. The link on our website is only for donations; it won't accept clinic fees. We no longer take cash at the mobile service.

responseBinding.questionText: information board

bindings.audiblePhrase: Begin in the car park in the south-west corner. Before you join the trail, look to the right, along the north edge of the parking area. The information board is there, beside the water tap. Do not confuse it with the small notice fixed to the toilets opposite. The main board carries today's closure, the ranger telephone number, and the route-check time, so each group should stop there.

responseBinding.questionText: tide gate

bindings.audiblePhrase: From the board, take the pale gravel path north-east. It reaches a low stone bridge over the stream. Cross the bridge but do not turn beside it; the narrow track following the bank serves the fields. Continue until the gravel becomes dark compacted earth at a wooden barrier on the coast. That barrier is the tide gate. You may hear the sea before you see it, but stay on the maintained surface until you reach the gate.

responseBinding.questionText: start of winter diversion

bindings.audiblePhrase: In summer the usual trail passes through that barrier and follows the shore. In winter, waves can cut off the beach with very little warning. The start of the winter diversion lies just before the gate, on its eastern side. Choose the narrower path bending inland, marked by two orange arrows. The broad track continuing north looks easier, but it leads towards the closed shore and must not be used.

responseBinding.questionText: emergency marker 3

bindings.audiblePhrase: The diversion climbs gradually between two fields. First you pass emergency marker two beside a dry-stone wall. That is not the point you need to label. Continue to the next bend, where a line of wind-shaped pine trees crosses your view. Immediately beyond the trees stands emergency marker three. The number is printed on both faces of the yellow post, so you can identify it when walking in either direction.

responseBinding.questionText: warming shelter

bindings.audiblePhrase: After marker three, the path descends towards two buildings near the service road. The larger grey building is the ranger store, which is locked to visitors. The warming shelter is the smaller building west of it, directly beside the walking path. It has a green roof and a covered doorway. If you reach the vehicle barrier by the store, you have gone too far east and should return to the path.

responseBinding.questionText: lookout point

bindings.audiblePhrase: Beyond the shelter, continue north and ignore the right-hand track dropping to the beach steps; those steps are closed. The safe trail curves left around the headland. It finishes at the lookout point, just south of the north arrow on your map. A rope barrier marks the end. There is no second exit beyond it, so anyone who is already tired should turn around at the shelter rather than attempt the final exposed section.

responseBinding.questionText: What should walkers check before leaving home?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Now, the safety details. Conditions on the headland can differ sharply from those in the nearest town, and clear sky above the car park tells you nothing about mist moving in from the water. Before leaving home, check the weather forecast specifically for this coast. If the warning is amber or red, postpone the walk rather than hoping it will improve.

responseBinding.questionText: What colour are the emergency markers?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Some older online photographs show red emergency posts, and a few faded red bases remain beside the path. Those markers were replaced two years ago: every current marker is yellow. In an emergency, quote the number on the nearest yellow post so the rescue team knows which approach to use.

responseBinding.questionText: What should walkers keep in a waterproof bag?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Carry drinking water and an extra warm layer, even for a short walk. A paper map is useful when reception is weak, but it cannot be used to call for help. Put a charged phone in a waterproof bag and check its battery before leaving. The rescue team asks you to protect that phone from spray because it provides both contact and a location reading.

responseBinding.questionText: What should walkers do if water covers the lower band at the tide gate?

bindings.audiblePhrase: At the tide gate, inspect the striped depth post before taking the inland turn. If water already covers the lower white band, turn back. Do not wait beside the gate for the level to drop, since the next surge may be higher, and never try to reach the diversion by stepping across wet rocks. The safe decision applies even when other walkers appear to be continuing.

responseBinding.questionText: Why do the group decide to use replica swatches?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: They avoid risk to collection objects.

bindings.audiblePhrase: That would still cause irreversible change to original material. When the same question can be answered with a replica, there is no ethical reason to consume a collection object. Use newly dyed wool swatches instead. You can make enough pieces for repetition, and their known recipes will help you interpret unexpected fading.

responseBinding.questionText: What will provide the main colour measurements?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Keep the photographs as a visual record, but don't make them the main data. Camera settings, processing, and screens can alter appearance. Take baseline and weekly colorimeter readings for repeatable numerical measurements. Average several points on each swatch so one dark fibre does not control the result.

responseBinding.questionText: What will be kept equal between the two lamp groups?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Equal hours are not necessarily equal exposure; one lamp may deliver more energy per hour. Adjust the duration so both groups receive the same total light dose. Then spectrum remains the independent variable. Include the calculation so another researcher can reproduce the schedule with lamps of different power.

responseBinding.questionText: What is the purpose of the dark control?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: to detect colour change not caused by light

bindings.audiblePhrase: No, the dark set has an analytical purpose. It reveals colour changes caused by reasons other than light, such as handling or dye instability. Keep it in the same room for comparable temperature and humidity, open it only for measurements, and handle it exactly like the illuminated swatches.

responseBinding.questionText: How will the students reduce the effect of shelf position?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Recording temperature is useful, but fixed samples would make location a hidden variable. Randomise the swatch positions each week, spreading shelf differences across treatments instead of confusing them with one lamp. Prepare the sequence in advance and retain it in the laboratory log.

responseBinding.questionText: What main limitation will the report acknowledge?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: Accelerated exposure may differ from slow gallery ageing.

bindings.audiblePhrase: You can compare treatments, but don't make that conversion. Short, intense exposure may not reproduce slow ageing under gallery conditions; reactions can change with intensity, temperature, and rest periods. State that as the main limitation and recommend longer observation before translating results into display years.

responseBinding.questionText: maintaining the dye preparation log

bindings.audiblePhrase: I've already tested the dye recipes, so I can maintain the preparation log. I'll enter fibre weight, dye concentration, bath temperature, and every batch number as the swatches are made. That will be more reliable than trying to reconstruct a batch from labels on the drying trays.

responseBinding.questionText: calibrating the colorimeter

bindings.audiblePhrase: Then I'll handle the colorimeter calibration. I used the same model during my placement. Before every weekly session I'll run the white-tile check, record the result, and repeat it if the instrument has drifted beyond the manufacturer's tolerance.

responseBinding.questionText: approving the maximum exposure ceiling

bindings.audiblePhrase: Good. The maximum exposure ceiling must be approved by me. It affects laboratory safety and sets the point beyond which the accelerated treatment would no longer be ethically or scientifically defensible. You can calculate the proposed dose, but place my name in the approval column.

responseBinding.questionText: contacting the textile workshop

bindings.audiblePhrase: That leaves the replica cloth. I met the textile workshop manager last term, so I'll contact the workshop and confirm the fibre specification, weave, quantity, and delivery date. I'll copy Lachlan into the message because he needs the cloth dimensions for the cutting plan.

responseBinding.questionText: Buoyancy is aided by ______ within the outer tissue.

bindings.audiblePhrase: The first transport filter is buoyancy. Size alone is a poor guide: a large seed whose tissues fill with water may sink, while a smaller one with persistent internal cavities can float. The crucial feature is air spaces within the outer tissue, which reduce overall density and keep the seed near the surface. Experiments use several intact samples because one cracked coat or unusually dense individual may behave differently.

responseBinding.questionText: A ______ slows the entry of sea water.

bindings.audiblePhrase: A second useful feature protects the embryo from immediate salt exposure. Abrasion and pre-existing cracks reduce that protection, and microscopic wear increases permeability during a long voyage. The barrier is a waxy coat, which slows the entry of sea water but never makes the seed permanently waterproof. Its value therefore depends on both its condition and the journey's length.

responseBinding.questionText: Seeds may be transported by ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Once afloat, a seed may move along a coast, enter open water, and approach another island. The main driver is ocean currents, not the wind direction observed on one day. Multi-year drifter records reveal recurring pathways, but they still express probabilities. Storms can push an individual away from the average route or hold it in circulating water much longer.

responseBinding.questionText: Storm debris can trap seeds at the ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Arrival creates another filter. Waves may throw seeds onto bare rock, where they dry or wash back immediately. Storm debris offers a better chance when it catches a seed at the tide line, above ordinary waves. Leaves and wood can provide shade and reduce movement, though heavy debris may bury the seed too deeply. A favourable feature at one stage can therefore create a later problem.

responseBinding.questionText: Rain supplies ______ that removes salt.

bindings.audiblePhrase: A stranded seed remains surrounded by salt. Repeated rain gradually lowers the concentration around the embryo and allows early metabolism to begin. The rain supplies fresh water, which drains through the upper beach and flushes the coat and sand. Tests that replace salt water instantly may exaggerate the benefit, because natural flushing is intermittent and depends on grain size and drainage.

responseBinding.questionText: The emerging root needs ______ for anchorage.

bindings.audiblePhrase: A viable, desalted seed still cannot establish on ground that shifts with every wave. The emerging root needs stable soil for anchorage, while organic matter retains moisture. The balance matters: saturated ground may lack oxygen, whereas rapidly draining sand leaves seedlings dry. Establishment also requires light and a period without renewed storm disturbance.

responseBinding.questionText: A flotation trial does not establish seed ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: The second half of the problem concerns evidence and its limits. A flotation trial demonstrates buoyancy, but buoyancy alone does not establish viability. A seed may remain on the surface for months while its embryo loses the ability to germinate. A stronger experiment tests germination after different periods in salt water and compares the result with an unexposed control, although even that design still simplifies the voyage.

responseBinding.questionText: Laboratory tanks simplify coastal ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Laboratory tanks are valuable because temperature, salinity, and duration can be repeated. Their weakness is that they simplify coastal turbulence. Real shores subject seeds to breaking waves, abrasion, burial, and repeated sinking and resurfacing. Wave simulators improve realism, but regular mechanical motion still lacks the unpredictable sequence of calm periods and storms.

responseBinding.questionText: Small field collections may introduce ______ bias.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Field collections have a different weakness. Researchers often recover only a few stranded seeds, so sampling can bias the apparent success rate. One storm may deposit many seeds on a monitored beach while a nearby shore receives none. Surveys should cover several sites and seasons, though large, recognisable seeds may still be reported more often than damaged specimens.

responseBinding.questionText: After germination, ______ may prevent permanent colonisation.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Finally, arrival and germination do not equal permanent colonisation. Existing plants may already occupy the available light, nutrients, water, and root space. In other words, competition can eliminate a young plant after every dispersal stage has apparently succeeded. Herbivory, disease, or the absence of pollinators may create further barriers, but competition is often the first ecological explanation tested when seedlings emerge and then disappear.
